source.title: Evolutionary Dynamics of Cancer: From Epigenetic Regulation to Cell Population Dynamics—Mathematical Model Framework, Applications, and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Consider a nonnegative density Q(t,x) of resting-phase stem cells indexed by a one-dimensional epigenetic state x in Ω⊂R+, with effective cytokine signal Q̂(t)=∫Ω Q(t,x)ζ(x)dx. In the delay-free version of the heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration model, ∂Q(t,x)/∂t = −Q(t,x)(β(Q̂(t),x)+κ(x)) + 2∫Ω β(Q̂(t),y)Q(t,y)e^{−μ(y)}p(x,y)dy, where β, κ, μ, ζ are nonnegative and p(x,y) is a transition probability satisfying 0≤p(x,y)≤1 and ∫Ω p(x,y)dx=1 for each mother state y. At steady state, Q(x) must solve L_{Q̂}[Q](x)=2∫Ω β(Q̂,y)e^{−μ(y)}p(x,y)Q(y)dy − (β(Q̂,x)+κ(x))Q(x)=0 together with Q̂=∫Ω Q(x)ζ(x)dx. In the general case, especially when β depends on x and p(x,y) depends on the mother state y, does there exist a positive eigenvalue Q̂ with a nonnegative eigenfunction Q(x), is the resulting steady state unique, and under what conditions is it stable?
accepted.context_brief: Steady states of the heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration equation

evidence.quote: The proposed mathematical framework (11) is a delay diﬀerential-integral equation that contains non-local transitions between diﬀerent epigenetic states. This type equation was not seen in most physical problems because of the principle of locality. Mathematically, there are many basic problems remain open for the equation (11).
For the simplicity, we omit the delay, and consider the equation with only one dimension epigenetic state. Hence, we have the following equation

Thus, the problem of existence and uniqueness of the steady state solution is reduced to a problem of ﬁnding a positive eigenvalue ˆQ of the operator L ˆQ so that the corresponding eigenfunction Q(x) is non-negative for all x∈ Ω.

If the transition probability p(x,y) is independent to the state of the mother cell, so that p(x,y) = p(x), the uniqueness and stability of the steady state were further discussed in [38]. However, it remains open questions for general cases. Biologically, the states of normal and precancerous correspond to stable steady states under diﬀerent conditions. Hence, mathematically identify the existence and stability of steady states are important for our understanding of the persistence of diﬀerent states.

accepted.question_text: Consider the same delay-free heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration model with total cell number Q(t)=∫Ω Q(t,x)dx, epigenetic-state fraction f(t,x)=Q(t,x)/Q(t), and multicellular entropy E(t)=−∫Ω f(t,x)log f(t,x)dx. For the induced dynamics of f(t,x), can the entropy derivative dE/dt be decomposed as epr−edr, where both the entropy production rate epr and the entropy dissipation rate edr are always nonnegative? More broadly, under what conditions on the rate functions and the nonlocal epigenetic transition probability p(x,y) is tissue development, and in particular cancer development, an entropy-increasing process?
accepted.context_brief: Entropy production and dissipation in epigenetically heterogeneous cell populations

evidence.quote: Let Q(t) = ∫Ω Q(t,x) for the total cell number at time t, and f(t,x) = Q(t,x) / Q(t) for the fraction of cells with given epigenetic state x. The entropy of the multicellular system at time t is deﬁned as E(t) = − ∫Ω f(t,x) log f(t,x)dx.

The entropy problem asks: how can we decompose the rate of entropy change into entropy production rate (epr) and entropy dissipate rate (edr) so that dE / dt = epr − edr, and both epr and edr are alway non-negative.

Solutions to this problem is essential to answer the question of how the entropy change along the process of tissue development. In particular, is cancer development a process of entropy increasing[15, 42]?
For the general situation, it is not know how the entropy production rate and dissipation rate should be deﬁned, and under which situation the development process is entropy increasing.

accepted.question_text: In the heterogeneous cancer-development model, x denotes a cellular epigenetic state, Q(t) or tumor volume gives total population size, f(t,x) gives the fraction of cells in state x, β, κ, μ, and ζ are the proliferation, differentiation/death/senescence, apoptosis, and cytokine-secretion rate functions, and p(x,y) is the probability that a daughter cell has state x given a mother cell with state y. Because p(x,y) is usually unknown and cannot be measured directly, how can experimental data such as imaging, liquid biopsies, biomarker measurements, single-cell sequencing, tissue, blood, and molecular data be used to infer p(x,y) and the rate functions β, κ, μ, and ζ well enough to build personalized predictive models and support optimal clinical decisions for cancer development?
accepted.context_brief: Inverse estimation of transition and rate functions from cancer data

evidence.quote: Moreover, to consider cell plasticity at each cell cycle, we introduce a transition function p(x, y) for the inheritance probability, which represent the probability that a daughter cell of state x comes from a mother cell of state y.
However, biologically we cannot measure this function directly, and do not know the possible form neither.

In the propose model, the transition probability function p(x,y) is usually not known, and cannot be measured directly from experiments. Hence, it is a challenge issue to estimate this transition function indirectly from experimental data.
Hence, the inverse problem of obtaining the rate functions β,κ,µ , and ζ, and the transition function p(x,y ) is essential for the development of personalized predictive model for cancer development.

In this way, we are trying to merger the propose model with the unwieldy multitude of dispersed data (imaging, tissue, blood, molecular) to estimate the personalized parameter and to generate optimal clinical decisions for each patient.

accepted.question_text: Assume epigenetic-state transition in the delay-free heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration model is local rather than global: p(x,y)=φ(y−x), where φ(r)>0 only for |r|<ε≪1, φ(r)≥0, ∫φ(r)dr=1, and the first two moments are a=∫rφ(r)dr and D=∫r²φ(r)dr. Let γ(q,x)=β(q,x)(2e^{−μ(x)}−1)−κ(x) be the net production rate. After substituting this local kernel into the normalized model and expanding to second order, the steady state f(x) satisfies a second-order differential equation involving β(λ,x)e^{−μ(x)}f(x), γ(λ,x)f(x), boundary conditions f(x)≥0 and ∫Ω f(x)dx=1, and the nonlinear eigenvalue relation λ=Q*∫Ω f(x)ζ(x)dx=Q̂. How can the steady-state existence, uniqueness, and stability problem, the entropy-decomposition problem, and the inverse-estimation problem be formulated and solved for this local-transition limit, including the resulting nonlinear eigenvalue problem for λ?
accepted.context_brief: Local transition approximation and nonlinear eigenvalue formulation

evidence.quote: In the equations (18) or (18)-(29), the epigenetic transition function p(x,y ) is global. Here, we assume that the epigenetic state can only have local transition, i.e., p(x,y ) = ϕ(y−x) so that ϕ(r)> 0 only when |r|<ϵ ≪ 1.

We further let a = ∫+∞−∞ rϕ(r)dr, D = ∫+∞−∞ r2ϕ(r)dr. Substituting (37) into (18), and expand the function ϕ to the second order approximation, we obtain the following close form diﬀerential-integral equation
From (40)-(42), the above questions of steady state solution, entropy problem, and inverse problem can also be formulated as the problem with local transition.
This equation deﬁnes a nonlinear eigenvalue problem for the eigenvalue λ = ˆfQ∗.

needs_review.question_text_raw: How cancers arise from normal tissues? Why is cancers so hard to treat?

evidence.quote: How cancers arise from normal tissues? Why is cancers so hard to treat? Despite many years researches, people know little about the evolutionary dynamics of cancer.

needs_review.question_text_raw: What are the routes from inflammation to cancer?

evidence.quote: Cancer risk increases strongly with the duration and extent of chronic inﬂammation[12, 5]. However, the routes from inﬂammation to cancer are poorly understood.

needs_review.question_text_raw: What is the mechanism of relapse after CD19-targeted CAR-T therapy for B-ALL?

evidence.quote: The majority of patients achieve a complete response following a single infusion of CD19-targeted CAR-T cells; however, many patients suﬀer relapse after therapy, and the underlying mechanism remains unclear.

needs_review.question_text_raw: How should the current equation be extended to include cell-to-cell interactions, immune cells, microenvironment, spatial information, and other factors for a more complete cancer-development model?

evidence.quote: Nevertheless, many other factors may also play important roles in cancer development, and are not included in the proposed model, such as the cell-to-cell interactions, immune cells, microenvironment, spatial information, etc. The current equation should be extended to included these factors for a more complete model.
